description: Categories for how commit messages express What changed and Why a skill modification was made. Independent of the skill-modification (pattern) taxonomy. Ported from the legacy RQ5 commit-message codebook (configs/commit_message_patterns.yaml). Subcategory patterns and examples are adapted from Tian et al., "What Makes a Good Commit Message?", ICSE 2022 (arXiv:2202.02974), Sec. 4.2.

what_expression_categories.coding_rule: Assign every What expression category supported by the commit messages. Use missing-what only when no What information is present.

allowed.label: summarize-skill-object-change
allowed.definition: Names the changed skill, skill file, resource, section, metadata field, script, or other skill artifact.

paper_patterns.name: Characteristics of changes
paper_patterns.definition: Highlights the characteristics of the current change and compares it with alternative implementations to summarize the change.
paper_patterns.example: "attempt at a 3rd I/O interface ... inspired by InputStream and OutputStream, but using growing buffers instead of byte arrays as the core data container"

paper_patterns.name: Object of change
paper_patterns.definition: Summarizes the change from the point of view of the code object that was changed (attribute, method, class, package, etc.). The most common subcategory, found in over half of commits.
paper_patterns.example: "remove creation of 'fat' jar..."

paper_patterns.name: Change list
paper_patterns.definition: Lists changes to several code objects, often involving one or more source files, typically as an itemized list.
paper_patterns.example: "this commit removes the following deprecated properties: 'server.connection-timeout' 'server.use-forward-headers' [...]"

paper_patterns.name: Contrast before and after
paper_patterns.definition: Contrasts the state of a code object before and after the change.
paper_patterns.example: "rename HeldCertificate.Builder.issuedBy() to signedBy()"

allowed.label: illustrate-skill-function
allowed.definition: Describes the changed skill behavior, agent capability, workflow effect, or user-facing function.

paper_patterns.name: Illustrate function
paper_patterns.definition: Summarizes and explains the change from a functional perspective rather than naming the specific code object changed, informing collaborators what new behavior was introduced.
paper_patterns.example: "Rename preferred-mapper property so it's clear it only applies to JSON"

allowed.label: describe-skill-implementation-principle
allowed.definition: Explains the technical mechanism, execution principle, or implementation strategy used by the skill change.

paper_patterns.name: Describe implementation principle
paper_patterns.definition: Describes the technical principle underpinning the change, i.e., the process by which the code executes correctly. The rarest What category (2.4% of analyzed commits).
paper_patterns.example: "SslContextBuilder using InetAddress.getByName(null) [...] On Android, null returns IPv6 loopback, which has the name 'ip6-localhost'"

allowed.label: missing-what
allowed.definition: Does not provide enough information to determine what changed in the skill.

paper_patterns.name: Missing what
paper_patterns.definition: Lacks any specification of what was changed, typically because the change is small/simple enough to be easily inferred (e.g., typo fixes, renames, whitespace changes).
paper_patterns.example: "fix typo a->an"

why_expression_categories.coding_rule: Assign every Why expression category supported by the commit messages. Use missing-why only when no Why information is present.

allowed.label: describe-skill-issue
allowed.definition: States a bug, error, failure, limitation, inconsistency, or other problem in a skill or its supporting artifacts.

paper_patterns.name: Describe error scenario
paper_patterns.definition: Directly describes where and how an error occurs; frequently indicates the source of a bug or defect, the steps to reproduce it, and its impact. The most common Why subcategory overall (19.8%).
paper_patterns.example: "As-is it throws unchecked exceptions on unexpected charsets. This is a problem because it can cause a misbehaving webserver to crash the client."

paper_patterns.name: Introduce issue report
paper_patterns.definition: Describes issues mainly by citing errors/defects/warnings recognized by quality assurance tools.
paper_patterns.example: "remove warnings found by errorprone. [...] CallTest.java:2056: warning: [UnnecessaryParentheses] Unnecessary use of grouping parentheses [...]"

paper_patterns.name: Describe shortcoming
paper_patterns.definition: Highlights shortcomings or weaknesses in the current implementation that motivate the commit.
paper_patterns.example: "I'm unhappy with java.io: No timeouts [...] Features like mark/reset and available() are clumsy [...]"

allowed.label: illustrate-skill-requirement
allowed.definition: States an external requirement, upstream change, platform constraint, user need, or usage scenario that required the skill change.

paper_patterns.name: Usage need
paper_patterns.definition: Describes specific needs or requirements of users, helping contributors understand the background and necessity of the change.
paper_patterns.example: "Error-prone only works on pre-12 at the moment and we need this configuration to apply for all JDKs"

paper_patterns.name: Out of date
paper_patterns.definition: Indicates the obsolescence of features or code, including deprecation and removal of unused code objects, or upgrades needed due to a dependency becoming obsolete.
paper_patterns.example: "Remove outdated key. The 'spring.metrics.export.redis.aggregate-key-pattern' is no longer defined but was still referenced in the documentation."

paper_patterns.name: Runtime or development environment change
paper_patterns.definition: Indicates an adaptation to the current development code or runtime environment, e.g., to accommodate API modifications.
paper_patterns.example: "API has changed, fixing the example"

allowed.label: describe-skill-objective
allowed.definition: States the intended goal, benefit, improvement, or desired outcome of the skill change.

paper_patterns.name: To fix defects
paper_patterns.definition: Makes explicit that the purpose of the change is to resolve a defect, clarifying how the proposed change will resolve it (as opposed to merely describing the error scenario).
paper_patterns.example: "Fix concurrent problem of zookeeper configcenter, wait to start until cache being fully populated"

paper_patterns.name: To make improvements
paper_patterns.definition: Directly describes the improvement of the implementation, e.g., functional or non-functional goals, often using phrases like "to do something" or "for something".
paper_patterns.example: "AndroidLog: Added [...] methods for easier subclassing."

allowed.label: imply-skill-necessity
allowed.definition: Implies the need for the skill change without explicitly stating an issue, requirement, or objective.

paper_patterns.name: Conventions and standards
paper_patterns.definition: Describes or refers to conventions or standards (project agreements or industry specifications) that are the basis for a change.
paper_patterns.example: "it is common to add tests to the same package as the class under test"

paper_patterns.name: Relation to prior commits
paper_patterns.definition: Explains the relationship between the current commit and prior commits already merged into the repository, e.g., fixing a problem introduced by a previous change.
paper_patterns.example: "the code was changed by commit <other url> but unfortunately the test was not part of the commit"

paper_patterns.name: Relation to an implemented feature
paper_patterns.definition: Relates the current change to an existing or upcoming feature, providing context as part of a larger operation underway or as preparation for a planned change.
paper_patterns.example: "a short step on the road to HTTP body format agnostic support"

paper_patterns.name: Improvements and benefits
paper_patterns.definition: Indirectly describes the need for a change by explaining the improvements and benefits it brings, sometimes comparing before/after state. The most common Imply Necessity subcategory (15.5%).
paper_patterns.example: "Use custom exception type [...]. Since we omit the stack trace, this more clearly indicates the source being from Retrofit's mock behavior"

allowed.label: missing-why
allowed.definition: Does not provide enough information to determine why the skill change was made.

paper_patterns.name: Test cases
paper_patterns.definition: Adds test cases to the repository; the rationale is common sense since adding tests for each feature is a widely shared convention.
paper_patterns.example: "tests for canceling async requests"

paper_patterns.name: Typographic fixes
paper_patterns.definition: Corrects typographical errors in code or documentation; the rationale (improving correctness/readability) is self-evident.
paper_patterns.example: "fix typo a->an"

paper_patterns.name: Text file changes
paper_patterns.definition: Changes made only to text files with specific functions, such as ChangeLog or README files.
paper_patterns.example: (changes confined to README/ChangeLog-type files, e.g., updating a changelog entry)

paper_patterns.name: Annotation changes
paper_patterns.definition: Changes the content of code annotations; since annotations exist to increase readability, the Why is common sense.
paper_patterns.example: "add docs about null responses"

paper_patterns.name: Code refactoring
paper_patterns.definition: Refactors or formats code, e.g., polishing, renaming, cleaning up, to improve readability without changing behavior.
paper_patterns.example: "Polish pom.xml. Apply consistent formatting, drop JDK 8 support and cleanup repo [...]"

paper_patterns.name: Version management
paper_patterns.definition: Involves version management such as updating version numbers; a routine step important for maintainability.
paper_patterns.example: "prepare version 2.8.1"
